transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (VP Eng, LumenPath), Maya Chen (Cloud Architect), Darren Lowe (Security)

Summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): initial intake about private deployment, they want EU residency, static egress IPs, transit gateway path not sure if peering enough, SOC two notes asked, asked for KMS integration details.

00:00 Sofia Martinez: hey everyone thanks for joining, um quick intros and then we'll jump into your network constraints, uh can I get a quick one-line from each of you?
00:12 Rajiv Patel: yea, hi, I'm Rajiv, VP Engineering at LumenPath, we're evaluating Redwood for host, dedicated or private, our primary constraint is that certain PII-based models have to remain in eu-west-1 and egress has to be controlled, we also have an existing Transit Gateway setup across accounts.
00:25 Maya Chen: Maya here, cloud architect — we're responsible for networking and infra, we need to understand IPs, DNS, and whether Redwood Private will live in our VPC or we connect back to Redwood's private VPCs.
00:37 Darren Lowe: Darren, security, I'm mostly interested in KMS integrations, audit logs, SOC 2 artifacts and key rotation cadence.
00:44 Sofia Martinez: great, so quick orientation — Redwood Private can run in a couple ways: one is our private control plane with private endpoints and you host the inference nodes in your VPC (customer-managed), another is a dedicated deployment where we provision a dedicated pool in our infra but expose private endpoints via VPC peering or TGW — there's some nuance, Ethan can dive in —
01:05 Ethan Cole: yeah, quick correction — there's a third mode where we do a co-managed model: you provide a peering/TGW and we run inference nodes in a customer-dedicated subnet inside your account (so compute sits in your VPC but control plane sits in our private plane), so it's like a hybrid. Apologies if I jumble the terms.
01:22 Rajiv Patel: okay can you clarify the differences in egress behavior for each? like where do outbound connections originate and can we guarantee static IPs?
01:33 Ethan Cole: short answer: if compute is inside your VPC, egress is under your control — you can NAT or egress through your proxy and have stable elastic IPs. If compute is in Redwood-managed infra we can allocate a stable egress IP block for your tenancy via NAT & egress proxy but that is a managed service and comes with reserved capacity pricing. There's also the TGW path where you peer and route — egress still depends on where compute sits.
01:58 Maya Chen: so for the hybrid where nodes run in our VPC, how are private endpoints exposed? do we create ENIs in our subnets or do you expect private link/private endpoints?
02:10 Ethan Cole: in our customer-hosted compute pattern we install a lightweight agent and provision ENIs in your subnets. Control plane calls back over private control connections; we hand you the endpoint DNS that resolves into your VPC; so traffic never goes over public internet. The alternative with TGW is we create a prefix list and route via TGW attachment.
02:30 Darren Lowe: any implications for cross-account roles or IAM? we use external ID and strict role chaining for any third-party services.
02:38 Sofia Martinez: we support cross-account IAM roles and you can require an assume role with external ID — standard pattern. We'll document the exact trust policy.
02:45 Rajiv Patel: EU residency — we need models and tokenization to remain in eu-west-1. Can Redwood host model shards in multiple regions? like if we need fallbacks during spike, we can't send eu data to us-east.
03:00 Ethan Cole: we have model pinning — you can pin inference to a model version running strictly in eu-west-1. We also have automatic fallbacks but for your case we can disable cross-region fallbacks. There is a tradeoff: capacity and latency during spikes, but we'll keep things region gated.
03:22 Maya Chen: and what about caching and KV cache? we use caching across requests and want to ensure KV cache doesn't replicate out of-region.
03:30 Ethan Cole: KV cache respects the deployment locality for Private; we don't shard KV to other regions unless you enable cross-region replication. So default: stays in-region.
03:38 Rajiv Patel: good. on egress IPs, we have vendor allowlists in place and need a small stable set of IPs, ideally a /28, is that doable if Redwood manages the egress?
03:49 Ethan Cole: possible but we typically allocate ranges based on the Dedicated tenancy size, a /28 is small but we'd evaluate. For customer-hosted compute it's trivial you just assign EIPs to NAT gateways. For us-managed we can commit to a set of IPs for an org-bound tenancy as part of the Dedicated contract.
04:10 Darren Lowe: what's the TLS termination and key custody model? do you hold TLS certs or do we bring our own?
04:18 Ethan Cole: TLS between control plane and customer is mutual TLS. For private deployments you can bring your own certs and we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key material. For hosted services we manage certs but support customer-provided certs in enterprise plans.
04:33 Rajiv Patel: SAML/SSO and RBAC — integration story?
04:36 Sofia Martinez: we integrate with SAML and OIDC, SCIM for provisioning, and you can map groups to RBAC roles in the Redwood Console. We'll share the SSO integration guide.
04:48 Maya Chen: network-wise the thing that worries us is DNS leakage — if we hand out a DNS name that resolves externally during failover it could leak. How do you manage split-horizon or private DNS?
04:58 Ethan Cole: we support split DNS via Route53 private hosted zones or via local DNS forwarding. For in-VPC ENIs we register A records into your private hosted zone. For TGW/peered setups we ask you to accept conditional forwarding or create private zones in the consumer account. There's a little nuance with cross-account private zones but it's manageable.
05:20 Rajiv Patel: any need for certificate validation in egress flows, like OCSP? sometimes our security team insists on egress to scanning proxies.
05:28 Ethan Cole: yes you can route egress through your inspection point — if compute is in your VPC that's straightforward. If it's our infra, we can set up a static NAT to your proxy but that'll add latency.
05:40 Maya Chen: got it. another question: Transit Gateway — we run TGW with multiple accounts attached and use route tables to segment traffic. Does Redwood require specific route table entries or particular blackhole avoidance?
05:53 Ethan Cole: we need a route in the TGW route table for the subnets where inference nodes live. We also recommend a dedicated TGW route table for the Redwood connection to avoid accidental route bleed. We'll supply the exact CIDRs and ANP (sorry AWS account numbers) for attachments.
06:12 Rajiv Patel: can you confirm support for shared services VPC patterns? we sometimes place NATs or proxies in a shared services account rather than per-app VPCs.
06:20 Ethan Cole: yes, we can route egress via a shared services NAT; you'll just need to ensure security groups and NACLs allow the flows. We can document recommended security group rules.
06:30 Darren Lowe: audit logs — we want full request/response metadata, but redacted PII. Is that supported?
06:36 Ethan Cole: we stream structured logs to your S3 or we can push to your SIEM via Kinesis/CloudWatch logs subscription; PII redaction is configurable at the request layer. We'll share the log schema.
06:48 Rajiv Patel: timelines — if we choose the customer-hosted compute model what's the approximate onboarding time?
06:54 Sofia Martinez: typically 3-6 weeks: networking & IAM set up 1-2 weeks, provision compute + test 1-2 weeks, security signoff and pilot 1-2 weeks. Dedicated managed-infra routes can be faster for small pilots.
07:08 Maya Chen: bandwidth — we do high-throughput inference, token volume could create significant egress out of our VPC, any recommended patterns to reduce cost?
07:18 Ethan Cole: recommend batching, prefix caching and KV cache warm-up; Redwood Optimize will suggest batch sizes and quantization profiles by workload. Locally hosting compute helps you control egress cost.
07:28 Rajiv Patel: any constraints with private link vs VPC peering? we like PrivateLink if it avoids route table complexity but not sure about IP preservation.
07:38 Ethan Cole: PrivateLink gives you a managed ENI per AZ and preserves IPs but it has per-GB costs; peering/TGW has different cost models. PrivateLink is usually used when customers don't want route changes in TGW.
07:52 Maya Chen: what about egress filtering at country level? we need to prevent data from leaving EU to US even for monitoring pings and health checks.
08:01 Ethan Cole: health checks and metrics can be routed to your monitoring endpoints inside the region; we can disable cross-region health pings. We'll also ensure metrics export endpoints are region localized.
08:12 Darren Lowe: compliance: do you provide SOC 2 Type II report evidence?
08:16 Sofia Martinez: yes — we'll share the SOC 2 artifacts under NDA and a compliance pack for Private deployments.
08:22 Rajiv Patel: interesting, ok one more: how do you handle failover if a whole AZ goes down? will traffic reroute to another AZ in the same region but same residency?
08:30 Ethan Cole: within-region AZ failover is supported; nodes are provisioned multi-AZ and KV cache is warmed across AZs in-region. We prefer AZ redundant patterns; cross-region failover is opt-in.
08:42 Maya Chen: any special network ports we need to open?
08:45 Ethan Cole: we'll provide a concise list — control plane ports (mutual TLS) and data plane ports; nothing fancy, mostly HTTPS + a couple of ephemeral ports for KV sync.
08:55 Rajiv Patel: scenario: we want to run a small pilot with 8 GPUs in eu-west-1, and have logs to our SIEM — can you outline next steps?
09:03 Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll send an onboarding checklist: networking CIDRs, TGW attachments if desired, account IDs, SAML metadata, and security contacts. We'll also attach a sample Terraform snippet for peering and ENI creation.
09:13 Maya Chen: would be helpful to see the sample tag and security group templates.
09:16 Ethan Cole: will include.
09:18 Darren Lowe: we'll review SOC 2 and KMS notes — if all good, procurement will start a PO.
09:23 Sofia Martinez: perfect. quick note we do have some internal docs: private deployment playbook, egress patterns (link in next steps).
09:30 Rajiv Patel: ok that's probably it from us — thanks.
09:32 Sofia Martinez: thanks everyone, recap: we'll send topology diagram & sample tf, SOC 2 artifacts, schedule SE deep dive week of Jan 11. Ethan will lead the technical session.
09:45 Ethan Cole: cool, I'll propose a couple times, also I'll draft a short one-page on egress IP options (managed vs customer NAT) so you can share with security.
09:53 Maya Chen: thanks, look forward to the deep dive.
09:55 Meeting end (approx)
